title: Indian-Origin Trisha Prabhu Built Anti-Cyberbullying Platform at 13, Now Leads Global Non-Profit
excerpt: From a Google Science Fair finalist to Harvard, Yale, Oxford, and Stanford graduate, Prabhu's ReThink technology has reached five million students across 134 countries.
body:
• Indian-American Trisha Prabhu created ReThink at age 13 — a mobile keyboard that detects offensive messages and prompts users to reconsider before posting, reducing willingness to send harmful content from 71% to just 4%.
  • The technology has reached over five million students across 1,500 schools in 134 countries, with more than 500,000 app downloads.
  • Prabhu, now 24, holds degrees from Harvard, Yale Law School, Oxford, and Stanford, and runs ReThink Citizens, a non-profit backed by a $50,000 grant from Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's Archewell Foundation.
  • She appeared on Shark Tank, received $100,000 from investors, and won the $300,000 Elevate Prize for social impact.

When Trisha Prabhu was 13 years old, she read about the death of Rebecca Sedwick, a 12-year-old student who died by suicide after relentless online harassment. The case changed the course of Prabhu's life. Within months, the Indian-American teenager had developed a technology designed to stop cyberbullying before it starts.

Flipping the Script on Prevention

Most anti-bullying tools at the time focused on the victim — blocking attackers or reporting to authorities. Prabhu asked a different question: could you reach the person sending the message before the damage was done?

https://x.com/NewIndianXpress/status/2089617839946956987

The answer became ReThink, a mobile keyboard that identifies potentially offensive phrases and pauses the sender with a simple prompt to reconsider. The app does not block the message. It interrupts the impulse, giving the person a moment to change their mind.

"I remember reading that story and thinking something's wrong here. Something is very wrong with our internet, with what it's become, and what we are sending young people into when they get a phone."

— Trisha Prabhu, founder of ReThink

The results were striking. In Prabhu's initial research, 71% of teenagers showed willingness to send aggressive messages without the alert. With the ReThink prompt, only 4% went ahead, according to The Harvard Crimson. Across broader use, young people stopped sending offensive messages in over 93% of instances when prompted to reconsider.

From Science Fair to Global Reach

Prabhu's concept earned her a spot as a 2013 Google Science Fair finalist at age 13. The recognition opened doors: she was invited to the White House, delivered a TED Talk in India, and landed $100,000 in funding from Shark Tank investors. In October 2020, she won the Elevate Prize, a $300,000 award selecting ten winners from roughly 1,300 applicants working on positive social change.

By that time, ReThink had already amassed over 500,000 downloads and worked with five million students across more than 1,500 schools in 134 countries.

An Academic Powerhouse

Now 24, Prabhu has assembled an academic record that matches her entrepreneurial ambitions. After graduating high school in 2018, she earned a bachelor's degree from Harvard University, a Doctor of Law from Yale Law School, a Master of Science and Master of Public Policy from the University of Oxford, and a Master of Business Administration from Stanford University's Graduate School of Business.

She remains the inventor, founder, and CEO of ReThink while also serving on the Board of Advisors at the Carson J. Bride Effect, a non-profit that protects children from technology-related risks.

Non-Profit Expansion and Royal Support

In 2023, Prabhu launched ReThink Citizens, a non-profit movement that tackles cyberbullying, promotes digital wellness, and empowers young people to build a more inclusive internet. The initiative received a $50,000 grant from Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's Archewell Foundation through the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund. The couple video-called Prabhu to congratulate her and publicly champion the organization's work.

What's Next

As cyberbullying continues to evolve alongside new platforms and AI-generated content, Prabhu's technology-first approach to prevention offers a model that scales. For the Indian diaspora, her trajectory — from a suburban teenager's science project to a globally recognized non-profit leader — underscores the outsized impact a single motivated person can have when technology meets purpose.
